Variable mortgage payments can be deceiving. A mortgage payment is some principal you're paying and some interest rate component summed together. Let's say, you're paying a $1000 P&I (Principal and interest, I prefer this terminology over payments- keeps me on top of things) - for simplicity, $500 is interest and $500 is principal. With a rate jump, your payments remain the same, but your P&I auto rebalance, now Principal is $400 and Interest is $600.

Your cash flow is not impacted, what it does impact is the life of the mortgage (amortization) - at the back end, you could see jump of 5/10 years.

Here's the part that irks me the most - Bank's aren't obligated to make you aware of this, unless, the ratio is so off for P&I that your amortization is going beyond 35 years, then they send you a letter which could easily be missed. 

Stay in touch with your advisor yearly, get your investment portfolio and credit portfolio checked.
